mappings.note: Cone mounted on a hemisphere with the two CURVED SURFACES set equal, giving r : h = 1 : sqrt(3). It is surface area of a combination (LO-2); no volume enters, so LO-3 is out.
Cone removed from a cylinder of the same base and height; remaining volume by subtraction. Composite volume, nothing melted.
Hemisphere surmounted by a cone, volumes added. Combination volume, so LO-3 not LO-2.
Liquid from a hemispherical bowl transferred into 72 cylindrical bottles with 10% lost - volume carried across a change of container shape, i.e. the conversion outcome, with the wastage as the twist.
Hemispheres scooped from both ends of a cylinder: total surface = cylinder curved + two hemisphere curved, the flat ends having gone. Surface of a composite, so LO-2.
Canal flow: a cuboidal column of water becomes a thin standing layer over a field. Volume conserved while the shape changes, C-7.3-LO-3, not a solid combination.

Water left = cylinder MINUS the dropped cone. The water never takes a new shape here - it simply overflows - so this is composite volume by subtraction (LO-3), unlike the rise-in-level items which are conversions.
Tent = cylinder plus conical top; canvas is the two CURVED surfaces added, then costed. Surface area of a combination.
Conical hole drilled in a cylinder; ratio of metal left to metal removed is a subtraction of volumes within one composite body. Drilling removes material, it does not recast it, so not C-7.3-LO-3.
Rain falling as a thin layer over a roof is collected as a cylinder of water; equating the two volumes across the change of shape gives the rainfall depth.
Copper in a hollow pipe = outer cylinder minus inner cylinder. Composite volume by subtraction, with a dm-to-cm unit step.
Volume of wood in a doubly scooped cylinder = cylinder minus two hemispheres. Composite VOLUME, which is what separates it from the surface-area version of the same toy.
Two separate cylinders compared on both curved surface area and volume. Comparison of one basic solid's formulas, never a combination.
Hemispherical bowl surmounted by a hollow cylinder; the visible area is the two curved surfaces added. Surface of a combination.
Cone on a hemisphere: total surface = 2 pi r^2 + pi r l, the shared circle being hidden. Composite surface area, and the cone's h comes from the total height.
Sphere melted and recast into many small cones; count from equating volumes.
Submerged sphere raises the water level: the sphere's volume reappears as a cylindrical slab of water. Volume conserved across shapes, the conversion outcome.
Water emptied from a conical vessel into a cylindrical one - the same body of liquid takes a new shape, which is exactly C-7.3-LO-3.
Earth dug from a cylindrical well is respread as an annular embankment; the WIDTH is the unknown. Volume conserved through a change of shape.
Displacement worked backwards: the rise is given and the vessel's diameter is unknown. Same volume-conservation idea as the forward version, so it shares C-7.3-LO-3 with it.
Well earth respread as an embankment of given width; here the HEIGHT is the unknown. Paired with the width version - same outcome, different unknown.

Two outcomes genuinely: the tub's ice cream is divided into ten cones (conversion, C-7.3-LO-3) and each portion is itself a cone-plus-hemisphere whose volume must be assembled (C-7.2-LO-3). Neither alone explains the solution.
Hemispherical tank drained at a fixed rate: one solid's capacity, converted to litres and divided by a rate. No second solid and no change of shape, so neither combination nor conversion applies.
504 cones melted into one sphere. The surface-area follow-up uses the recast sphere's radius, so the conversion is the governing outcome rather than any surface outcome.
Three quarters of a conical vessel emptied into a cylinder; the water changes shape, so conversion rather than combination.
